summary:
Telling the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars NASA has left rovers, landers, a helicopter and other science tools across the solar system. These machines finished their missions, but their stories are scattered across technical archives. The problem we saw: kids are curious about space, but this history isn’t written for them. Our question: how can we make kids care about machines that stopped working years ago?
A storytelling website where every spacemachine becomes a character. Each retired machine introduces itself to kids in the first person: “Hi, I’m Sojourner, the first rover on Mars!”. Kids explore, read, play and remember, instead of just reading facts. Made for ages [7–12], with simple language, bright visuals and short stories. Every fact on the site comes from official NASA data.
details: Somewhere on Mars, a rover built to last 90 days kept driving for 14 years, and its tracks are still there. Tracing Footprints lets children aged 7–12 follow them. It is an interactive website, in Ukrainian and English, about the robots humanity has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, told in words a child can follow and built to be explored by hand. Every mission has a short illustrated story, a timeline and a 3D model to spin and zoom, and the machines that moved come alive in our 3D route stories: Opportunity drives its full 45 km across real Martian terrain, tiny Sojourner circles its lander, and the Ingenuity helicopter lifts off for all 72 of its flights over Jezero crater, pausing at the big moments to tell what happened there. Nothing is invented: the routes come from NASA’s mission maps and rover telemetry, the craters from orbital elevation data, and where real data does not exist the page says so, because we refuse to teach children something untrue. We built it with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, rendered the worlds with Three.js and React Three Fiber, prepared models in Blender, designed in Figma, wrote Python scripts to cut gigabytes of terrain into chapters light enough for a school computer, and used Claude Code as a coding assistant. The engine behind the stories knows nothing about any single mission, so a new one can be added with a data file and one line of code. Our hope is simple: a child spends twenty minutes here and leaves knowing that exploration is real, that machines built for a week can last for years, and that science is an adventure they can join.
